pages.text:
Saturday number three began with a plan to stay awake, which sounds brave but mostly means standing in the hallway holding a bag of pretzels until your eyes feel like sandpaper. I propped myself against the wall next to the clock, keeping my back straight even though my knees were locked up and my eyes were burning.

I did not blink. I did not yawn. I did not think about the moving truck.

At 11:58, I waited, watching the second hand creep around the face of the clock. The tick-tock sound was loud in the quiet house, like a tiny wooden hammer tapping on a table. I squeezed the pretzels in my hand until they crumbled, watching the dust fall to the floor.

At 11:59, the little door in the clock face clicked open. Gerald popped out. He did not cuckoo. He just looked at me with his angry painted eyebrows, clicked the door shut, and vanished into the wood.

I blinked, hard and fast, trying to see if the world was still there.

The hallway was empty. The pretzels were gone from my hand. I was on my bed.

"RAAAAWR."

Gus was on my chest again. I looked at the wall and took a pencil from my pocket. I scratched a single vertical line into the wood. One mark. One day.

I was not going to lose my mind. I was going to keep score.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy in a red hoodie, stands propped against a hallway wall holding a bag of pretzels, looking exhausted; a small cuckoo clock with an angry painted bird is visible on the wall nearby.

pages.text:
Saturday number four was about testing the limits. I went into the kitchen and picked up Mom’s favorite blue mug, the one with the chipped handle that looked like it had been chewed by a very angry squirrel. I looked around to make sure she wasn’t watching, then I let go of it.

It hit the tile and broke into three clean pieces. I felt terrible for about a minute, and then I went to bed. At 6:47 the next morning the mug was back on its shelf, whole, chipped handle and all, as if nothing had ever happened to it.

I looked at my thumb. The splinter from the cardboard box that had been stuck there for the last two days was gone. My hand was smooth. I ate seven slices of cold pizza for breakfast, and my stomach did not growl or hurt. It was just a stomach, which was actually kind of nice until I realized it meant I couldn't use it as an excuse to leave the table.

I went to the closet and wrote it down on the wall in pencil.

RULE 1: Everything resets except me.

I looked at the two vertical lines I had drawn. The day was a tape I could rewind, but the problem was that I was still stuck in the middle of the song, unable to skip to the part where it ends.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy, stares in shock at a blue mug bouncing on a kitchen tile floor, while a chubby corgi watches from the corner; a cardboard box sits open on the counter.

pages.text:
On Saturday number five, I decided to try talking to someone. It seemed like the most logical move, like saving a game before the boss level. If I could tell one person, maybe I could get help.

At the kitchen table, I leaned in close. "Mom, I need you to listen. I’m living the same day over and over. I know it sounds crazy, but I’ve been here before."

Mom stopped writing on her clipboard. She reached over and touched my forehead. Her palm was cool and dry.

"Max, you’re feverish," she said, not looking up. "Are you worried about the move?"

I tried Dad. "Dude, big changes are hard. I feel like I’m stuck in a loop."

Dad nodded, wiping his hands on his fish apron. "I feel that way every time the Wi-Fi lags. It’s a common feeling, Max."

I tried Tessa. She was tapping her drumsticks on the table. The rhythm was steady and annoying.

"I’m trapped in time," I said.

"Take a lap," she said, without looking at me. "You need to calm down."

RULE 2: Nobody believes me. Nobody remembers me trying.

I sat back. The silence in the kitchen was heavy.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy, sits at a kitchen table looking frustrated, while his mother, a woman with a clipboard, checks his forehead; his father in a fish apron looks on, and his sister taps drumsticks on the table.

pages.text:
Saturday number six was about running away. Not from the house, but from the block. I figured if I crossed the town line, maybe the loop would break. Maybe the day would end there.

I walked until the houses turned into fields, and then until my shoes were covered in mud. Finally, I saw the sign that said DUNMORE, OHIO. I stood right next to it and waited for something.

Nothing happened.

I walked back, and when I got to the door, it was 11:58. The clock was still on the wall. Gerald was still in his box. I went to my room.

RULE 3: The day ends wherever I am.
RULE 4: Nothing I do sticks.

I looked at my list. Four lines. Four days. I had a whole Saturday to do whatever I wanted, with no consequences, no moving truck, and no goodbye.

A slow, bad idea started to grin at me. It was the kind of grin that tastes like sour candy.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy in a red hoodie, stands next to a wooden town sign in a grassy field, looking tired and muddy; the sky is dark blue with early stars appearing.

pages.text:
This is a good place to stop and tell you what I knew and what I didn’t.

I knew every second of this day. I knew when the toast would burn. I knew when the sprinkler would soak the mailman. I knew exactly where the ice cream truck would turn the corner. I had the map. I had the keys.

I did not know why. The clock did not speak. The bird did not explain. The magic was a closed door with no handle.

I did not know how many Saturdays there would be. Five? Fifty? A thousand? The pencil marks on my wall were a tiny, fragile thing against the whole of the day.

And I did not know the most important thing yet. I didn’t know that you can be in the same day a hundred times and still not have been in it once. I thought the loop was a prison. I was wrong. It was a playground with no rules, and I was the only kid who knew where the sandbox was.

Then I thought of something foolish. Something bright.

What if I just had fun?
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy, sits on his bed looking thoughtful, a pencil in his hand; a small cuckoo clock on the wall has its door open, revealing the small painted bird inside.
